question: Assume today is 2026-08-23. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of live births in South Korea in July 2026, as it will be first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release.

target.what: Number of live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first published in Statistics Korea's monthly Population Trends (인구동향) release
target.publisher: Statistics Korea (KOSTAT), monthly Population Trends / 인구동향
target.cadence: monthly, typically released around the 4th week of the following month (so July 2026 data would first appear ~late August 2026)
target.caveats: Counts births by month of occurrence (occurrence-based), registered residents of Korea; excludes stillbirths. First-reported figure is provisional and subject to later revision. If the July 2026 release has not yet occurred by cutoff, the target is a forecast of a not-yet-published figure. Alternati

candidates.hypothesis: July 2026 births follow the recent level and seasonal pattern of monthly births; July is typically a high-birth month relative to June. Recent monthly values (2024-2026) plus a July seasonal factor give a baseline.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live births for South Korea from KOSTAT Population Trends for Jan 2023 through the latest month published before cutoff (likely June 2026), plus July values for 2023, 2024, 2025 to estimate the June-to-July seasonal ratio.

candidates.hypothesis: Administrative resident-registration birth counts (주민등록 출생) track statistical live births closely and are published with a shorter lag, providing a near-contemporaneous proxy for July 2026.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly 주민등록 출생자 수 (행정안전부) for 2025 and 2026 through July 2026, and the historical ratio of KOSTAT live births to resident-registration births by month.

candidates.hypothesis: YTD births through mid-2026 plus a July share of the annual total (from prior years) yields July 2026; annual total times July share is an alternative route.
candidates.data_to_find: Cumulative Jan-Jun 2026 births (if published), annual 2025 births, and the historical July share of annual births (2015-2025).

candidates.hypothesis: Births = women of childbearing age × age-specific fertility rates; monthly births can be built from the female population by age and recent TFR/ASFR, adjusted for seasonality.
candidates.data_to_find: Female population by single year of age (2026), recent age-specific fertility rates or TFR (2024-2025), and monthly seasonal birth distribution.

candidates.hypothesis: Recent policy expansions (parental leave, birth grants, marriage incentives) and calendar effects (Lunar New Year timing, marriage cohort shifts) alter the level and month-to-month path of births in 2026.
candidates.data_to_find: Evidence on 2024-2026 birth-support policy changes, marriage registrations 2024-2025 (leading indicator ~9-12 months), and any reported monthly birth trend commentary in 2026.

candidates.hypothesis: KOSTAT or research institutes may publish 2026 monthly or quarterly birth projections or nowcasts that constrain July 2026.
candidates.data_to_find: Any 2026 birth projections, quarterly birth estimates, or monthly nowcasts published before cutoff by KOSTAT, KDI, or demographic researchers.

assessment.note: Same article, same underlying KOSTAT annual release: 2025 births 254,500, +16,100 (+6.8%) vs 2024. Internally consistent (254,500 - 16,100 = 238,400 for 2024). One measurement, not three independent confirmations.

TFR path 0.72 (2023) -> 0.75 (2024) -> 0.80 (2025 provisional) is reported identically by two outlets drawing on the same KOSTAT figures; corroboration of the fertility-recovery narrative, not independent measurement.

Monthly shares of 2025 births from one article: Jan 9.5%, Sep 8.8%, Jul/Oct 8.6%, Feb/Jun/Dec 7.9%. These are shares of the same annual total, so they are mutually consistent by construction and must sum with the unlisted months to 100%.

Birth-order split: 158,700 first + 79,300 second = 238,000, i.e. 62.4% + 31.2% = 93.6% with 6.4% third-or-later. Consistent with p1's 254,500 total only approximately (238,000/254,500 = 93.5%), so the order counts appear to be a slightly different tabulation/vintage; use only as context.

Q1 2026 resident-registration births 73,742 (+15% yoy) and January 2026 official births 26,916 (+11.7% yoy) point the same way: a strong early-2026 upswing. Different definitions (registration vs occurrence-based) but same direction; the 2% typical gap (p30) is the bridge.

Registered pregnancies Apr 2025–Mar 2026 = 351,000, +16% yoy, with a 10–15% non-live-birth loss rate. This is a leading indicator for births roughly Jul 2025–Jun 2026, i.e. it covers the target month only at its very tail; it supports an elevated 2026 level but cannot pin July alone.
Marriages 239,000 (2019) -> 191,000 (2022) -> ~240,000 (2025). The 2023–2025 marriage rebound is the demographic driver behind the 2025–2026 birth increase; consistent with p1/p2 and p25/p26.
Population decline and ageing context; consistent with low but rising fertility. Not numerically usable for a monthly birth count.
p1 (annual 2025 total) and p6 (July share of 2025) combine to give July 2025 births ≈ 254,500 × 8.6% ≈ 21,900; this is the natural base for a yoy-scaled July 2026 estimate.

January 2026 = 26,916 (+11.7%) implies January 2025 ≈ 24,100, which is 9.5% of 254,500 ≈ 24,180 — consistent. So the 2026 uplift is real and roughly +10–15% yoy in the months observed; July 2026 should be scaled from July 2025 by a similar but possibly attenuating factor.

kept.rationale: 2026 opened strong: January 2026 official births +11.7% yoy (p32) and Q1 2026 registrations +15% (p29); 2025 as a whole was +6.8% (p3). kept.applies_when: July 2026 births track the early-2026 upturn with some moderation; used to scale the July 2025 level.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that the 2026 upturn faded by mid-year (e.g. Q2 2026 registrations near flat) or that July 2025 was an unusually high base.

kept.name: 2026 annual live births as a multiple of 2025 annual live births
kept.rationale: 2025 was 254,500 (p1); early-2026 growth of ~+11.7% (p32) suggests a further rise, tempered because January is seasonally strong and the upturn may fade. Centred ~+5% over 2025, range +1% to +10%.
kept.applies_when: 2026 annual births continue the 2025 recovery at a moderate pace.
kept.falsified_by: Mid-2026 monthly data showing births flat or declining versus 2025.

kept.name: Two-year yoy change factor from July 2024 to July 2026
kept.rationale: July 2025 is not directly observed; July 2024 = 20,601 (p34). 2025 annual births rose +6.8% (p3) and 2026 early months rose ~+11.7% (p32), so cumulative two-year growth from July 2024 to July 2026 is plausibly ~+12%, with a wide range.
kept.applies_when: July births grew roughly in line with the annual 2025 and early-2026 trends.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that July 2025 was unusually high or low relative to the 2025 annual trend.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
